A SIGMA ALUMNUS AT THE
CONVENTION
By Stephen Wati
WHEN
I received an urgent ap
peal to write my impressions
of the 1940 Psi Upsilon Convention,
I was reminded of the words of
Brother Spaeth, Tau '88:
"There are men that can write.
There are men than can fight
There are men that can sing a
gay ditty;
There are men that look wise
Tho' they're fools in disguise.
Then too there are fools that are
witty."
Under which heading I may excel,
it is distinctly not that of composi
tion; I flunked this miserably under
Bancroft in '84 and I have wisely
refrained from attempting anything
of the sort since that memorable in
stance. Yet comes this appea so
pressing, so flattering, and I have
one day to write the story!
I remember very clearly certain
highlights of my flrst convention at
Hartford. I was a Brown student at
the time. I can't remember what chap
ter was host or the exact date and I
fail to recall any of the various busi
ness meetings. But I do remember
the banquet held at the leading
hotel. Governor Hawley of Con
necticut presided. On my left was
Charles Dudley Warner who read a
poem. On that occasion I was certain
ly filled with Sigma pep and I didn't
get it at Heublein's across the way.
From that time to this, for one
reason or another, I don't seem to
have attended any other conven
tions. The years rolled by until June.

Thursday and Friday luncheons

in East Providence. All luncheons
were buffet and well served; attend
ance was large, reminiscing was at
its best. Friday afternoon the Con
vention picture was taken. Saturday
evening, the banquet picture.
Thursday, on the first day of the
Convention, a buffet supper and
smoker with entertainment was held
at the Biltmore Hotel. Jovial groups
were gathered about chatting cheer
ily. It was there that the little book
of tickets for the various Conventionsponsored affairs was exchanged for
the modest stipend charged for the
entire three day program. At the
entrance guests registered and were
handed their name pins. After sup
per we repaired with the smokes to
the large banquet hall and there
witnessed one of the most remark
able feats of legerdemain I've ever
seen. One memory test would take
another page to describe.

ciation meeting at the chapter house

grounds, which are magnificent.

marks by other

ers at the head

Anthem the cur

down on the 107th National Con
vention.
The most interesting incident of
the three days in Providence, but
strictly pertaining to the Sigma, was
the dedication of Memorial Gate on
the George Street side of the univer
sity grounds. Dean Otis E. Randall
made the dedication. The gate was
received by Brown's president,
Henry M. Wriston.
This report is not in any way
meant to be a convention record,
rather is it a simple narrative from
the memory of the bully time one
old brother had in his old home town
with a bunch of the best pals on
earth. In conclusion, I must add
that this three day celebration did
me more good than any other of like
duration for many years.

UNDERGRADUATE POLL FAVORS
WILLKIE, 9-1; DRAFT, 3-1
To the questions "Who do you want
for president, Willkie or Roosevelt.''"
and "Do you favor the draft.''", 21
chapters out of 27 reported the follow
ing: 747 for Willkie, 85 for Roosevelt,
and 28 indefinite; 677 undergraduates
out of 860 are for the draft.
These results will give alumni some
idea of how American undergraduates
are thinking today. Specifically, if Psi U
undergraduates had their way, Willkie
would be the next president of the
United States by a 9 to 1 choice. The
draft went over by a 3 to 1 margin. Of
those eligible (252) for the draft 4 out
of 5 undergraduates favor joining Uncle
Sam's army. Of the 21 American chap
ters responding to this call, only one,
Sigma, was unanimously for Willkie.
But three. Kappa, Tau and Epsilon,
were 100% behind the draft. Here '^is
how some of the chapters feel about the
draft :
Theta: The U. S. is growing soft, its
citizens are willing to take everything
from the State and give nothing in re
turn ... at least we should be willing
to protect our benefactors. . . . Some
undergraduates fear being called out of
college before their four years are com
plete. To stop their education for army
service would probably result in failure
to finish. Perhaps they would be more
valuable to the country with a complete
four year education. Those favoring the
draft say that the average student faces
no real hardship. Thus a year in the
army would do them good. It would be
a rude awakening from the soft collegi
ate life to the routine of the army. This
is harsh but necessary.
Others cry that the draft is against
"the American way of life" and is an
encroachment upon civil liberties and
rights. They say the draft reflects the
dictatorial methods of the countries aim
ing toward complete world supremacyIn rebuttal: the only way to beat a
dictatorship or to preserve this "Ameri
can way of life" is by the method used
in the totalitarian states. When the
danger passes the pre-World War . . .
situation can be restored. We should
not be caught in the maelstrom like
France and England.
Feeling runs high among some that
they should be prepared to take care of
themselves in a conflict involving the
U. S. Ability to handle a gun, protect
the U. S., and deal effectively with an
enemy is more important than being led
to battle totally ignorant of the art of
modern warfare. In this age there will
be no whole year as in 1917-1918, when
the U. S. can prepare itself for war un
molested.
Theta opinion : Unsettled, as many did
not seem to realize the importance of
the present crisis we are facing.
Delta: Apprehensive of tendency of
employers failing to hire men of draft
age. Those in favor: Best way to raise
army. The law is fair in its attempt to
overcome the obstacles arising over jobs
and college courses.
Delta opinion: those favoring draft
seem to be in least danger of being
drafted. Undergraduates fear draft
more than working people.
Sigma: World affairs have caused a
change of attitude at the house this
fall. Baseball statistics are subordinated
to anti-aircraft statistics. National poli
tics takes precedence over football bull
sessions. But there is little talk of the
draft. Those venturing an opinion say:
A large military machine is essential
for the safety of the U. S. and military
training alone can insure personal safety.
However, there is much speculation on
how well the New Deal is capable of
making adequate defense preparations.
